---
title: "Positional Encoding"
description: "Information added to a sequence representation so a model can distinguish token positions and order."
term: "Positional Encoding"
letter: "P"
category: "Deep Learning"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Attention can compare tokens without naturally knowing which came first.
Positional encoding gives a model information about where tokens occur,
helping it distinguish sequences such as “dog bites person” from “person
bites dog.”

## Technical explanation

In a Transformer, position information is combined with token
representations or incorporated into attention. The original Transformer
used fixed sine and cosine functions of position and dimension. Other
architectures learn position embeddings or use relative-position and rotary
schemes.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Position representations affect how models use order, handle longer inputs,
and transfer to sequence lengths not seen during training. The choice is
part of model architecture and can influence both quality and context-length
behavior.

## How it works

With additive encoding, a position vector is added to each token embedding:
$\mathbf{h}_i=\mathbf{e}_i+\mathbf{p}_i$. Attention then uses these
position-aware representations. Relative schemes instead encode distance
between positions in token representations or attention scores.

## Practical example

At inference, a language model assigns an embedding to each input token and
adds or applies its position information before self-attention. The
resulting attention can use both token identity and sequence order.

## Common misconceptions

- Positional encoding is not the same as a token embedding: one represents
  sequence location, the other represents token content.
- There is no single positional scheme used by every Transformer.
